questions.stem: What does mitosis produce?
options: Two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell
Four daughter cells each with half the parent's chromosomes
Two daughter cells each with half the parent's chromosomes
Four daughter cells genetically different from each other
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two nuclei with the same number and type of chromosomes as the original cell. Four genetically different haploid cells are the products of meiosis.

questions.stem: Which list gives roles of mitosis in the human body?
options: Growth, repair of tissue and replacing worn-out cells
Producing sperm and eggs for sexual reproduction
Halving the chromosome number before fertilisation
Creating genetic variation among the body's cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis makes identical cells for growth, healing wounds and replacing cells such as skin and blood cells. Gamete production and halving the chromosome number are roles of meiosis.

questions.stem: A cell is preparing to divide by mitosis. In which part of the cell cycle does it copy its DNA?
options: Prophase of mitosis
Anaphase of mitosis
Telophase and cytokinesis
The S phase of interphase
questions.explanation: DNA is copied during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids when mitosis begins. No DNA replication occurs during mitosis itself.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the stages of mitosis in order?
options: Metaphase, prophase, telophase, anaphase
Prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase
Interphase, telophase, metaphase, anaphase
Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense in prophase, line up at the equator in metaphase, have their chromatids pulled apart in anaphase, and are enclosed in new nuclei in telophase. Interphase is not part of mitosis.

questions.stem: What happens during anaphase of mitosis?
options: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell
Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange sections of DNA
Chromosomes line up in single file along the middle of the cell
The nuclear membrane re-forms around each group of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids of each chromosome to opposite poles, so each new cell gets an identical set. Pairing of homologues happens only in meiosis.

questions.stem: A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromatids does it contain at metaphase of mitosis?
questions.explanation: DNA replication in interphase turns each of the 46 chromosomes into two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids. The chromosome number is still 46 because sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase.

questions.stem: Why is it important that DNA replication occurs before chromosomes separate in mitosis?
options: So each daughter cell receives half the DNA, keeping the chromosome number low
So that the extra DNA can be broken down for energy during cytokinesis
So that crossing over can create new allele combinations in the daughters
So each daughter cell receives a complete, identical copy of every chromosome
questions.explanation: Replication produces two identical chromatids per chromosome; separating them gives each daughter cell the full genetic information. Crossing over is a feature of meiosis, not mitosis.

questions.stem: Which description of cytokinesis is correct?
options: The replication of DNA before the cell divides
The pairing of homologous chromosomes during meiosis
The condensing of chromosomes at the start of mitosis
Division of the cytoplasm to form two separate cells
questions.explanation: Cytokinesis follows nuclear division: in animal cells the membrane pinches inwards to split the cytoplasm into two cells. DNA replication happens earlier, in interphase.

questions.stem: What two properties define a stem cell?
options: It has no nucleus and can move freely between different tissues
It is fully specialised and can no longer divide in the body
It divides repeatedly by mitosis and can become specialised cells
It can divide by meiosis and produce haploid cells of many types
questions.explanation: Stem cells self-renew through mitosis and are unspecialised, so they can develop into specialised cell types. Specialised cells such as neurons have usually lost this ability.

questions.stem: Which cell is totipotent?
options: A cell from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst
A skin stem cell
A zygote
An adult bone marrow stem cell
questions.explanation: A totipotent cell can give rise to every cell type, including the placenta and other extra-embryonic tissues; the zygote and the cells of the first few divisions are totipotent. Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent.

questions.stem: Embryonic stem cells from the inner cell mass can become any cell of the body but not the placenta. What is this level of potency?
options: Multipotent
Unipotent
Pluripotent
Totipotent
questions.explanation: Pluripotent cells can form all the body's cell types from the three germ layers, but not extra-embryonic tissues. Totipotent cells can form both.

questions.stem: Stem cells in red bone marrow produce red cells, white cells and platelets but not neurons. What is their potency?
options: Pluripotent
Totipotent
Unipotent
Multipotent
questions.explanation: Multipotent adult stem cells give rise to a limited range of related cell types, here the blood cells. Pluripotent cells could form any body cell, including neurons.

questions.stem: A patient with leukaemia receives a transplant of blood-forming stem cells from a matched donor. Why can this treat the disease?
options: The donor cells are totipotent and so can rebuild every tissue the cancer damaged
The donor cells release antibiotics that kill the cancerous white blood cells
The donor cells divide and differentiate to restore healthy blood cells
The donor cells fuse with cancer cells and correct the mutations in their DNA
questions.explanation: After the patient's diseased marrow is destroyed, transplanted multipotent stem cells settle in the marrow and produce all the blood cell types. They are not totipotent and do not repair cancer cells' DNA.

questions.stem: Why are induced pluripotent stem cells made from a patient's own skin cells of interest for therapy?
options: They are taken from embryos, so they have the widest potency of any stem cell type
They can form many cell types and are less likely to be rejected by the patient
They are totipotent and so can form a whole new organ, including its placental tissues
They never divide once implanted, so they cannot form tumours in the patient's body
questions.explanation: Induced pluripotent stem cells are adult cells reprogrammed to a pluripotent state; because they carry the patient's own antigens, rejection is less likely and no embryo is used.

questions.stem: What is a tumour?
options: A group of cells that has stopped dividing completely
An infection of a tissue by bacteria or viruses
A mass of fluid trapped in the lymph nodes
A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division
questions.explanation: When cells divide without the normal controls of the cell cycle, they form a mass called a tumour. Cancer is not an infection, though some viruses can increase cancer risk.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign tumour?
options: Malignant tumours grow slowly and stay enclosed in a capsule at one site
Benign tumours always spread through the blood to form secondary tumours
Benign tumours are caused by mutations; malignant tumours are not
Malignant tumour cells invade nearby tissue and can spread around the body
questions.explanation: Malignant (cancerous) tumours invade surrounding tissues and can metastasise through blood or lymph. Benign tumours stay localised, though they can still cause harm by pressing on organs.

questions.stem: Mutations in the gene for a protein that normally stops damaged cells from dividing are found in many cancers. Why does this mutation increase the risk of cancer?
options: Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing instead of being halted or destroyed
Cells stop dividing entirely, so damaged tissue cannot be repaired by mitosis
Cells start dividing by meiosis instead of mitosis and become haploid
Cells lose all their DNA, so they cannot produce the proteins they need
questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor proteins check the cell cycle and halt or destroy cells with damaged DNA. When the gene is mutated, damaged cells divide unchecked and accumulate further mutations.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle factor is most strongly linked with an increased risk of lung cancer?
options: Eating a high-fibre diet
Drinking plenty of water
Regular physical activity
Smoking tobacco
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains many carcinogens that damage DNA in lung cells, causing mutations that can lead to uncontrolled division. The other choices are associated with lower cancer risk, not higher.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes does a normal human gamete contain?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid, containing one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. Fertilisation restores the diploid number of 46.

questions.stem: Why is meiosis called a reduction division?
options: It removes harmful alleles from the chromosomes of gametes
It halves the chromosome number from diploid to haploid
It reduces the size of the cell by removing its cytoplasm
It reduces the amount of DNA in each chromosome by half
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so each cell receives one of each pair and the chromosome number falls from 46 to 23. Each chromosome still carries its full DNA.

questions.stem: What separates during meiosis I and meiosis II?
options: Meiosis I: sister chromatids. Meiosis II: homologous chromosomes
Meiosis I and II: homologous chromosomes both times
Meiosis I and II: sister chromatids both times
Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes. Meiosis II: sister chromatids
questions.explanation: In meiosis I homologous chromosomes are pulled apart, halving the number; in meiosis II the sister chromatids separate, as in mitosis. The result is four haploid cells.

questions.stem: Which events of meiosis are listed in the correct order?
options: DNA replication, first division, second DNA replication, second division
DNA replication, pairing of homologous chromosomes, first division, second division
Pairing of homologous chromosomes, first division, DNA replication, second division
First division, DNA replication, second division, pairing of homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated once in interphase, homologues pair in prophase I, then two successive divisions follow without further replication. That is how four haploid cells come from one diploid cell.

questions.stem: What is crossing over, and when does it occur?
options: Movement of whole chromosomes between two different cells during telophase I
Exchange of DNA between non-homologous chromosomes during mitosis in body cells
Exchange of DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologues in prophase I
Exchange of DNA between sister chromatids of one chromosome during anaphase II
questions.explanation: When homologues pair in prophase I, non-sister chromatids can break and rejoin at chiasmata, swapping sections and creating new combinations of alleles on each chromosome.

questions.stem: Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of chromosomes can random assortment produce in human gametes?
options: 23 × 2, which is 46
23 squared, which is 529
2 to the power of 46, about 70 trillion
2 to the power of 23, about 8 million
questions.explanation: Each of the 23 homologous pairs lines up independently at metaphase I, so there are 2²³ (about 8.4 million) possible combinations. Crossing over and fertilisation increase variety further.

questions.stem: Which description of non-disjunction is correct?
options: The exchange of sections between homologous chromosomes in meiosis
The random alignment of homologous pairs at the cell's equator
The fusion of two haploid gametes to form a diploid zygote
Failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate in meiosis
questions.explanation: If homologues (meiosis I) or chromatids (meiosis II) fail to separate, some gametes receive an extra chromosome and others lack one. Exchange of sections is crossing over.

questions.stem: An egg with two copies of chromosome 21 is fertilised by a normal sperm. What is the outcome?
options: A zygote with 92 chromosomes, because it is tetraploid
A zygote with 47 chromosomes and trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
A zygote with 45 chromosomes and monosomy of 21
A zygote with 46 chromosomes, because the sperm loses one
questions.explanation: The egg contributes 24 chromosomes (including two copies of 21) and the sperm 23, giving 47 with three copies of chromosome 21. This is the usual cause of Down syndrome.

questions.stem: A person has the karyotype 45,X. Which error most likely produced this?
options: Random assortment giving two X chromosomes to one of the gametes
An extra round of mitosis in the zygote after fertilisation
Non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes in one parent's meiosis
Crossing over between the X and Y chromosomes in the father
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction can leave a gamete with no sex chromosome; fused with a gamete carrying one X, the zygote has 45 chromosomes. This is Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: Which statement about the products of mitosis and meiosis in humans is correct?
options: Both give four cells, but only mitosis involves DNA replication
Mitosis gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis gives four varied haploid cells
Mitosis gives four varied haploid cells; meiosis gives two identical diploid cells
Both give two cells, but only meiosis cells are genetically identical
questions.explanation: Mitosis is one division producing identical diploid body cells; meiosis is two divisions producing four genetically different haploid gametes. Both are preceded by one round of DNA replication.

questions.stem: How do the differences between mitosis and meiosis suit their roles in the body?
options: Identical cells keep tissues uniform; varied haploid gametes keep the chromosome number and add variety
Identical gametes ensure offspring resemble parents; varied body cells allow tissues to adapt quickly
Haploid body cells save energy in growth; diploid gametes give offspring a double set of genes
Varied body cells protect against cancer; identical gametes prevent inherited genetic disease
questions.explanation: Body tissues need cells with the same genetic information, which mitosis provides. Meiosis halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores 46, and its shuffling creates genetically unique offspring.

questions.stem: Which combination of sex chromosomes does a typical human male have?
options: YY
XO
XY
XX
questions.explanation: Typical males are XY and typical females are XX. All eggs carry an X, while sperm carry either an X or a Y.

questions.stem: Why is the chance of a child being male about 50%?
options: The mother's hormones decide the sex at the time of implantation
The sex depends on which ovary released the egg that cycle
Half of a man's sperm carry an X and half carry a Y chromosome
Half of a woman's eggs carry an X and half carry a Y chromosome
questions.explanation: Meiosis in males separates the X and Y, giving equal numbers of X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm. Every egg carries an X, so the sperm determines the child's sex.

questions.stem: Two siblings with the same parents, who are not identical twins, differ genetically. Which processes explain this?
options: Epigenetic marks that change the base sequence of each sibling's DNA
Crossing over and random assortment in meiosis, and chance fertilisation
Mitosis in the zygote and DNA replication errors in every body cell
Non-disjunction in every gamete and the loss of mitochondrial DNA
questions.explanation: Each gamete has a unique mix of alleles due to crossing over and random assortment, and which sperm fertilises which egg is a matter of chance. Non-disjunction is an occasional error, not the source of normal variation.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same genotype, but non-identical twins do not. Why?
options: Identical twins come from one zygote that splits; non-identical twins come from two eggs fertilised by two sperm
Identical twins come from two eggs fertilised by one sperm; non-identical twins come from one egg and two sperm
Identical twins come from two zygotes that fuse; non-identical twins come from one zygote that divides by meiosis
Identical twins have no crossing over in their cells; non-identical twins have crossing over in every cell
questions.explanation: Monozygotic twins form when one early embryo separates into two, so their DNA is identical. Dizygotic twins develop from two separate eggs and sperm and are as alike as ordinary siblings.

questions.stem: In a cell undergoing meiosis, a homologous pair carries alleles A and a for one gene. Without crossing over, which gametes can this pair produce?
options: Gametes with A only, because A is the dominant allele
Gametes with neither allele, because the pair is lost
Gametes with A and gametes with a, in equal numbers
Gametes with both A and a, as each gamete gets both
questions.explanation: Homologues separate in meiosis I, so each gamete receives one of the pair and therefore one allele. Half the gametes carry A and half carry a, regardless of dominance.

questions.stem: What is the diploid number of chromosomes in a human body cell?
questions.explanation: Human body cells are diploid, with 23 pairs (46 chromosomes): 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Gametes are haploid with 23.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a pair of homologous chromosomes in a body cell?
options: A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the same genes at the same loci
Two identical copies of one chromosome joined at the centromere after replication
Any two chromosomes of the same length, whether or not they carry the same genes
Chromosomes found only in gametes, carrying alleles that are always identical
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes match in size, centromere position and gene sequence, but may carry different alleles because one came from each parent. Two identical copies joined at the centromere are sister chromatids.

questions.stem: Skin cells divide often throughout life, but most mature neurons rarely or never divide. Which consequence follows?
options: Neurons are more likely than skin cells to form tumours in adults
Skin cells have more chromosomes than neurons in the same person
Neurons must be replaced by meiosis whenever they are damaged
Damage to the brain is repaired far less readily than a graze on the skin
questions.explanation: Because most mature neurons do not divide, lost neurons are not readily replaced by mitosis, so nervous tissue repairs poorly. Skin is constantly renewed by mitosis in its basal layer.
